lines.text: In 1970, a new American home cost about $24,000. Today the typical new home costs about $410,000.
lines.say: In nineteen seventy, a new American home cost about twenty-four thousand dollars. Today the typical new home costs about four hundred and ten thousand.

lines.text: Sure, everything costs more than in 1970. But homes have gotten more expensive even compared to paychecks.
lines.say: Sure, everything costs more than in 1970. But homes have gotten more expensive even compared to paychecks.

lines.text: So what happened? Today we'll take it apart: prices, supply, interest rates, and who gets squeezed.
lines.say: So what happened? Today we'll take it apart: prices, supply, interest rates, and who gets squeezed.

lines.text: Chapter 1. The price tag.
lines.say: Chapter one. The price tag.

lines.text: Let's compare homes to incomes, because that's what really matters.
lines.say: Let's compare homes to incomes, because that's what really matters.

lines.text: In 1970, the median household earned about $8,730 a year.
lines.say: In nineteen seventy, the median household earned about eight thousand seven hundred thirty dollars a year.

lines.text: A new home cost about 2.7 years of that income.
lines.say: A new home cost about two point seven years of that income.

lines.text: In 2025, the median household earned $87,460, a record high.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, the median household earned eighty-seven thousand four hundred sixty dollars, a record high.

lines.text: But the typical new home now costs about 4.7 years of income.
lines.say: But the typical new home now costs about four point seven years of income.

scene.title: Years of income for a new home

lines.text: Incomes went up about ten times. New home prices went up about seventeen times.
lines.say: Incomes went up about ten times. New home prices went up about seventeen times.

lines.text: And that's just the price. Most people don't pay cash. They borrow, and borrowing has its own story.
lines.say: And that's just the price. Most people don't pay cash. They borrow, and borrowing has its own story.

lines.text: Chapter 2. Not enough homes.
lines.say: Chapter two. Not enough homes.

lines.text: The simplest reason prices climb: more people want homes than there are homes.
lines.say: The simplest reason prices climb: more people want homes than there are homes.

lines.text: After the 2008 crash, builders slammed on the brakes.
lines.say: After the 2008 crash, builders slammed on the brakes.

lines.text: In 2009, housing starts fell to their lowest level since the government began tracking them in 1959.
lines.say: In two thousand nine, housing starts fell to their lowest level since the government began tracking them in nineteen fifty-nine.

lines.text: Construction took about a decade to recover, and all those missing years add up.
lines.say: Construction took about a decade to recover, and all those missing years add up.

lines.text: How big is the gap? Estimates vary. Freddie Mac puts the shortage around 3.7 million homes.
lines.say: How big is the gap? Estimates vary. Freddie Mac puts the shortage around three point seven million homes.

lines.text: Zillow's estimate is even higher: about 4.7 million.
lines.say: Zillow's estimate is even higher. About four point seven million.

lines.text: Building is also slow and expensive: land, labor, materials, and local rules about what can be built where.
lines.say: Building is also slow and expensive: land, labor, materials, and local rules about what can be built where.

lines.text: When there aren't enough homes, buyers bid against each other, and prices rise.
lines.say: When there aren't enough homes, buyers bid against each other, and prices rise.

lines.text: Chapter 3. The rate rollercoaster.
lines.say: Chapter three. The rate rollercoaster.

lines.text: Now the loan. Mortgage rates decide how much house a monthly payment can buy.
lines.say: Now the loan. Mortgage rates decide how much house a monthly payment can buy.

lines.text: Here's the 30-year rate, averaged by year, from Freddie Mac's survey.
lines.say: Here's the thirty-year rate, averaged by year, from Freddie Mac's survey.

lines.text: In 1981, it averaged over 16%. Brutal.
lines.say: In nineteen eighty-one, it averaged over sixteen percent. Brutal.

lines.text: Then it fell for forty years, and in 2021 it averaged under 3%.
lines.say: Then it fell for forty years, and in twenty twenty-one it averaged under three percent.

lines.text: In January 2021, it hit a record low of 2.65%.
lines.say: In January twenty twenty-one, it hit a record low of two point six five percent.

lines.text: Cheap money let buyers borrow more, and prices jumped.
lines.say: Cheap money let buyers borrow more, and prices jumped.

lines.text: Then inflation hit, rates shot up, and this September the 30-year average passed 7% again.
lines.say: Then inflation hit, rates shot up, and this September the thirty-year average passed seven percent again.

lines.text: Chapter 4. The payment math.
lines.say: Chapter four. The payment math.

lines.text: Let's make it real. Say you borrow $400,000 for 30 years.
lines.say: Let's make it real. Say you borrow four hundred thousand dollars for thirty years.

lines.text: At 3%, the monthly payment for principal and interest is about $1,686.
lines.say: At three percent, the monthly payment for principal and interest is about sixteen hundred eighty-six dollars.

lines.text: At 7.03%, the same loan costs about $2,669 a month.
lines.say: At seven point oh three percent, the same loan costs about twenty-six hundred sixty-nine dollars a month.

lines.text: That's almost $1,000 more every month, for the exact same house.
lines.say: That's almost a thousand dollars more every month, for the exact same house.

lines.text: And that's before property taxes and insurance, which have been rising too.
lines.say: And that's before property taxes and insurance, which have been rising too.

lines.text: Chapter 5. Why nobody's selling.
lines.say: Chapter five. Why nobody's selling.

lines.text: Here's the strangest part. High rates should cool prices. So why haven't they fallen much?
lines.say: Here's the strangest part. High rates should cool prices. So why haven't they fallen much?

lines.text: Because millions of owners locked in cheap mortgages, and they don't want to give them up.
lines.say: Because millions of owners locked in cheap mortgages, and they don't want to give them up.

lines.text: Roughly four in five mortgages still have a rate below 6%.
lines.say: Roughly four in five mortgages still have a rate below six percent.

lines.text: Selling would mean trading a 3% loan for a 7% one. So many owners just stay put.
lines.say: Selling would mean trading a three percent loan for a seven percent one. So many owners just stay put.

lines.text: Fewer sellers means fewer homes on the market, which keeps prices high even when rates are high.
lines.say: Fewer sellers means fewer homes on the market, which keeps prices high even when rates are high.

lines.text: Chapter 6. Who gets squeezed.
lines.say: Chapter six. Who gets squeezed.

lines.text: Put it together: high prices, high rates, few listings. Who feels it most? First-time buyers.
lines.say: Put it together: high prices, high rates, few listings. Who feels it most? First-time buyers.

lines.text: In the latest National Association of Realtors survey, first-time buyers were just 21% of buyers, the lowest share on record.
lines.say: In the latest National Association of Realtors survey, first-time buyers were just twenty-one percent of buyers, the lowest share on record.

lines.text: And the typical first-time buyer was 40 years old, also a record.
lines.say: And the typical first-time buyer was forty years old, also a record.

lines.text: Many are waiting longer, saving bigger down payments, or renting for more years.

lines.say: Chapter seven. The whole thing in one screen.

scene.title: The whole thing in one screen

lines.text: So why did houses get so expensive? Four reasons.
lines.say: So why did houses get so expensive? Four reasons.

lines.text: One: prices rose much faster than paychecks, from 2.7 years of income to 4.7.
lines.say: One. Prices rose much faster than paychecks, from two point seven years of income to four point seven.

lines.text: Two: America didn't build enough homes after 2008.
lines.say: Two. America didn't build enough homes after two thousand eight.

lines.text: Three: mortgage rates more than doubled from their 2021 lows.
lines.say: Three. Mortgage rates more than doubled from their twenty twenty-one lows.

lines.text: Four: owners with cheap loans are staying put, so fewer homes come up for sale.
lines.say: Four. Owners with cheap loans are staying put, so fewer homes come up for sale.

lines.text: Nobody can promise where prices go next. But now you know what's moving them.

post.title: Why Houses Got So Expensive (The Full Story)
post.yt_desc:
In 1970 a new home cost about 2.7 years of the median household's income. Today it's about 4.7 years. We take the housing market apart: prices vs paychecks, the shortage that started after 2008, the mortgage-rate rollercoaster from 16% to 2.65% to 7%, the payment math on a $400,000 loan, the lock-in effect, and why first-time buyers are older than ever.
